Estate Planning

Gain Clarity For Your Future. Protect What Matters.

Estate planning is about more than deciding what happens to your assets after your death. A thoughtful estate plan can help protect the people you care about, provide guidance during periods of incapacity, and ensure that important financial and healthcare decisions are made according to your wishes.

At AC Law Firm, we help individuals and families create estate plans tailored to their lives, priorities, and goals. Whether you are creating your first estate plan, experiencing a major life change, or reviewing documents you prepared years ago, we provide clear, practical guidance throughout the process.

Estate Planning Services

Depending on your circumstances and objectives, your estate plan may include:

Last Will and Testament

A will allows you to direct how certain assets should be distributed after your death, nominate a Personal Representative to administer your estate, and address other important matters, including the nomination of guardians for minor children.

Revocable Living Trusts

A revocable living trust can provide a structured way to manage and transfer assets during your lifetime and after your death. Trust planning may also help with incapacity planning, privacy, and avoiding probate for assets that are properly transferred to the trust.

Powers of Attorney

A financial power of attorney allows you to designate someone you trust to handle financial and legal matters on your behalf if circumstances arise in which you are unable—or unavailable—to handle them yourself.

Advance Medical Directives

An advance medical directive allows you to communicate your healthcare preferences and designate an individual to make healthcare decisions on your behalf when necessary.

Estate Plan Reviews and Updates

Estate plans should evolve as your life changes. Marriage, divorce, the birth of a child, the purchase of property, changes in financial circumstances, relocation, or the death of a loved one may create a reason to revisit your existing plan.

Who Should Have an Estate Plan?

Estate planning is not reserved for individuals with significant wealth. If you own property, have financial accounts, have children or other loved ones you want to protect, own a business, or simply want greater control over future financial and healthcare decisions, an estate plan can provide important protections.

Planning can be particularly important after major life events such as:

  • Marriage or divorce
  • Having or adopting a child
  • Purchasing a home
  • Starting or acquiring a business
  • Accumulating significant assets
  • Moving to a new state
  • Changes in family relationships
  • Receiving an inheritance
  • A significant change in health or circumstances

A Plan Designed Around Your Life

No two families are exactly alike, and an estate plan should reflect more than a collection of standard documents.

Our process begins with understanding your family, your assets, your concerns, and what you want your plan to accomplish. From there, we identify the planning tools appropriate for your circumstances and explain your options in straightforward terms so that you can make informed decisions.

The goal is not simply to prepare documents. It is to create a coordinated plan that reflects your wishes and provides clear direction when it matters most.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need both a will and a trust?

Not everyone needs a trust, and having a trust does not necessarily eliminate the need for a will. The appropriate combination of documents depends on your assets, family circumstances, planning objectives, and how you want those assets managed and transferred.

Can an estate plan help avoid probate?

Certain planning strategies may allow assets to pass outside of probate, including properly funded trusts, beneficiary designations, and certain forms of joint ownership. Whether avoiding probate should be a primary objective depends on your individual circumstances.

When should I update my estate plan?

You should consider reviewing your estate plan after significant life or financial changes. Even without a major event, periodically reviewing your documents can help ensure that your fiduciary appointments, beneficiary choices, and planning objectives continue to reflect your wishes.

What happens if I become incapacitated?

A comprehensive estate plan can designate trusted individuals to assist with financial and healthcare decisions if you are unable to make or communicate those decisions yourself. Planning in advance can reduce uncertainty for both you and your family.
